extracted.subtask_description: Curating, using, and evaluating style guides and topical reporting resources for newsroom use; includes guidance on choosing authoritative sources and special-topic (sensitive/community) style guidance. Useful for reporters, editors and newsrooms updating house style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt and maintain a style guide
rubrics_metrics.description: Style guides are a handy resource for any journalist. Many newsrooms subscribe to the Associated Press Stylebook or similar, which may be supplemented by a shorter 'house style' document. Larger newsrooms may develop their own guide in-house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a primary, widely accepted stylebook (e.g., AP) and supplement with a concise house style. Keep the house style consistent across the newsroom and develop in-house guidance for recurring local or organizational needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep style guides current with evolving language and society
rubrics_metrics.description: All [style guides] evolve along with society and modern language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly review and update house style and reference choices to reflect changes in acceptable terminology, emerging identity language, and societal norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate multiple perspectives; question terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: These resources can be helpful ... Remember that these are only suggested approaches. It may be good to evaluate multiple perspectives. You should always question terms and try to understand why something is or isn’t appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult more than one style/resource when terms are contested. Ask who is affected by the language and why a term is recommended or discouraged before adopting it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay attention to the source and potential bias or PR interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay attention to the source, as some are from independent journalist organizations, some are academic, and others may have a PR interest (ex: government or advocacy groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether guidance comes from journalist-led bodies, academic research, advocacy groups, government, or industry; consider how that provenance might influence recommendations and whether supplemental, independent guidance is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: When no topic-specific guide exists, consult general/comprehensive resources
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can’t find a guide for a specific topic, check the 'general/comprehensive' section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comprehensive diversity/inclusion style guides (e.g., Conscious Style Guide, The Diversity Style Guide) as fallback references and seek additional specialized resources as they become available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use community-specific style guides for culturally competent reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use guides produced by community-specific journalist associations (examples: AAJA, NABJ, NAHJ, AMEJA, Indigenous Journalists Association, NLGJA) for coverage of particular communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting on racial, ethnic, religious, LGBTQIA+, Native/Indigenous, or other identity communities, consult the relevant association’s style guide to avoid common errors and ensure respectful, accurate terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision with firearms and weapon terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: NOTE: Journalists unfamiliar with firearms and other weapons are prone to misusing technical terminology that has very precise meanings, sometimes with serious legal implications. A bullet is NOT a round, a magazine is NOT a clip, a revolver is NOT a pistol, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify weapon-related terms with credible subject-matter sources; do not rely on colloquial or imprecise language because mislabeling can have legal and factual consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specialized guidance for suicide and include safety resources
rubrics_metrics.description: NOTE: It’s a good practice to include an editor’s note in stories about suicide that directs people to a 24/7 suicide hotline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow established suicide-reporting recommendations (e.g., Reporting on Suicide, SAMHSA guidance). Include crisis hotline information and other safety resources, avoid sensational detail, and follow recommended phrasing to minimize harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-reference mental disability guidance with mental health resources
rubrics_metrics.description: NOTE: For mental disability, also see additional guides under 'mental health' below.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering mental disability topics, consult both disability-specific and mental-health-specific resources to ensure accurate, non-stigmatizing terminology and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of veterans’ sensitivities in terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: NOTE: Veterans (particularly Marines) frequently object to terms like 'ex-Marine' and occasionally 'former Marine,' though it’s broadly understood the latter means no disrespect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use terminology preferred by the veterans/community in question; when uncertain, ask or follow guidance in veterans/military-specific style references. Consider whether deviations from AP style enhance or undermine respectful accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider whether non-journalist or advocacy sources are appropriate supplements
rubrics_metrics.description: Some listed guides are from non-journalist sources (e.g., BishopFox for cybersecurity, GLAAD — advocacy, SAMHSA — government).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat non-journalist or advocacy-origin guidance as potentially valuable subject-matter information but evaluate for advocacy perspective and adapt language recommendations to journalistic norms as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply trauma-informed reporting practices and attend to vicarious trauma
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the intense nature of some topics, journalists may find themselves dealing with trauma. Vicarious trauma is real trauma. If you need help, a good place to start is the Journalist Trauma Support Network from the Dart Center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow trauma-informed journalism guides for interviewing and storytelling about victims and disasters; provide newsroom support and resources to reporters covering traumatic events to mitigate vicarious trauma.
